articles.title: Feriado da Consciência Negra em SP: veja o que abre e fecha e como ficam Metrô, trens, rodízio e serviços públicos | G1
articles.standfirst: Linha 3-Vermelha ficará fechada por quase duas horas na sexta-feira (20); rodízio será suspenso e cerca de 2,5 milhões de veículos devem circular pelas rodovias de acesso à capital.
articles.summary: Linha 3-Vermelha ficará fechada por quase duas horas na sexta-feira (20); rodízio será suspenso e cerca de 2,5 milhões de veículos devem circular pelas rodovias de acesso à capital.
articles.body:
Trânsito intenso na Radial Leste, em São Paulo — Foto: FÁBIO VIEIRA/FOTORUA/ESTADÃO CONTEÚDO

O feriado do Dia da Consciência Negra, celebrado nesta sexta-feira (20), vai alterar o funcionamento do transporte público, do trânsito e de diversos serviços na cidade de São Paulo e na região metropolitana. Entre as principais mudanças estão a interrupção temporária da Linha 3-Vermelha do Metrô, alterações na circulação dos trens e a suspensão do rodízio municipal de veículos.

Para quem pretende viajar durante o feriado prolongado, a expectativa é de que 2,5 milhões de veículos utilizem as rodovias de acesso à capital, segundo as concessionárias. Já os terminais rodoviários Tietê, Barra Funda e Jabaquara devem receber cerca de 474 mil passageiros entre quinta-feira (19) e segunda-feira (23).

Na capital, serviços essenciais de saúde funcionarão normalmente, enquanto equipamentos públicos terão horários diferenciados. Os parques municipais permanecerão abertos, e a Avenida Paulista e as ruas da Liberdade serão destinadas exclusivamente a pedestres e ciclistas na sexta-feira e no domingo.

Confira abaixo o que muda durante o feriado:

A Linha 3-Vermelha ficará fechada entre 4h40 e 6h30 desta sexta-feira (20) para a realização de testes do novo sistema de sinalização e controle de trens, conhecido como CBTC.

Durante a interrupção, os passageiros poderão utilizar gratuitamente os ônibus do sistema Paese, que circularão entre as estações Corinthians-Itaquera e Palmeiras-Barra Funda.

Outra alternativa será a Linha 11-Coral da CPTM, que terá reforço na frota durante o período.

Após as 6h30, a Linha 3-Vermelha voltará a funcionar normalmente, até a meia-noite.

As demais linhas administradas pelo Metrô terão a seguinte programação:

Linha 1-Azul: funcionamento normal, com oferta de trens equivalente à de domingo.

Linha 2-Verde: funcionamento normal, com oferta de trens equivalente à de domingo.

Linha 15-Prata: funcionamento normal, com oferta de trens equivalente à de domingo.

Linha 17-Ouro: operação transitória, das 6h às 22h.

Na madrugada de sábado (21) para domingo (22), o Metrô manterá a operação experimental de 24 horas nas linhas 1-Azul, 2-Verde, 3-Vermelha e 15-Prata. As estações permanecerão abertas para embarque e desembarque durante toda a madrugada.

A operação experimental está prevista para continuar até o fim de janeiro de 2027.

As linhas de trem e metrô administradas pela iniciativa privada também terão operação diferenciada no feriado.

Linha 4-Amarela: intervalos de aproximadamente 5 minutos.

Linha 5-Lilás: intervalos médios de 6 minutos.

Linha 7-Rubi: circulação por via única entre Franco da Rocha e Baltazar Fidélis, com embarque e desembarque na mesma plataforma, nos dois sentidos. Alguns trens no sentido Jundiaí terão Caieiras como destino final, exigindo transferência. Os intervalos serão de 12,5 minutos entre Palmeiras-Barra Funda e Caieiras e de 40 minutos entre Caieiras e Jundiaí.

Linha 8-Diamante: intervalos de aproximadamente 10 minutos até as 22h e de 15 minutos depois desse horário.

Linha 9-Esmeralda: intervalos de cerca de 10 minutos até as 8h, de 15 minutos entre 8h e 18h e de 10 minutos após as 18h. Depois das 22h, haverá trens retornando na estação Presidente Altino.

Linha 13-Jade: intervalos de 12 minutos durante todo o dia.

O Expresso Aeroporto, que liga a capital ao Aeroporto Internacional de São Paulo, em Guarulhos, terá partidas a cada 30 minutos na sexta-feira (20).

No sábado (21), os trens partirão a cada uma hora.

No domingo (22), o serviço será suspenso das 9h até a meia-noite, devido a trabalhos de manutenção da CPTM na região da Estação Brás. Entre 5h e 8h30, as partidas ocorrerão a cada 30 minutos.

Durante a suspensão, os passageiros poderão utilizar as linhas 12-Safira e 13-Jade como alternativas para chegar ao aeroporto.

Os ônibus metropolitanos que atendem a Grande São Paulo circularão na sexta-feira (20) com a programação habitual de domingo.

No sábado (21) e no domingo (22), a operação ocorrerá normalmente, de acordo com a programação de cada dia.

O rodízio municipal de veículos estará suspenso na sexta-feira (20), em razão do feriado.

Também não estarão em vigor as seguintes restrições:

Zona de Máxima Restrição à Circulação de Caminhões (ZMRC);

Zona de Máxima Restrição aos Fretados (ZMRF);

Restrições de circulação nas faixas exclusivas de ônibus, que estarão liberadas.

A Zona Azul funcionará conforme a sinalização em locais específicos, como o entorno dos parques Ibirapuera, Água Branca, Aclimação e Piqueri, além da Praça Charles Miller, do Museu do Ipiranga e da região do Mercado Municipal da Cantareira.

A ciclofaixa de lazer também será ativada na sexta-feira.

A Companhia de Engenharia de Tráfego (CET) realizará a Operação Estrada entre quinta-feira (19) e segunda-feira (23), para monitorar o trânsito de saída e retorno à capital.

A expectativa é de que 2,5 milhões de veículos utilizem as rodovias de acesso à cidade, em direção ao litoral e ao interior, durante o feriado prolongado.

Em todo o estado, a Agência de Transporte do Estado de São Paulo (Artesp) estima a circulação de 18,9 milhões de veículos pelas rodovias concedidas entre os dias 19 e 23.

Entre os sistemas com maior movimentação prevista estão:

Anhanguera-Bandeirantes: 2,69 milhões de veículos;

No Sistema Anchieta-Imigrantes, poderão ser adotadas operações especiais de reversão de pistas, como os esquemas 7x3 e 2x8, de acordo com o movimento.

Na Rodovia dos Tamoios, serão mantidas duas pistas para descida e duas para subida. Já na Padre Manuel da Nóbrega, poderá haver liberação do acostamento em trechos específicos, enquanto a Mogi-Bertioga poderá receber operações de reversão de pista.

As concessionárias reforçarão as equipes de atendimento, com guinchos, ambulâncias e veículos de inspeção, além de restringir obras e serviços de rotina nos horários de maior movimento.

Os terminais rodoviários Tietê, Barra Funda e Jabaquara devem receber aproximadamente 474 mil passageiros entre quinta-feira (19) e segunda-feira (23).

Segundo a Socicam, concessionária responsável pelos três terminais, estão previstos 118 mil embarques somente entre quinta e sexta-feira.

O dia de maior movimento deve ser esta quinta-feira (19), com aproximadamente 62 mil embarques em 1.962 ônibus.

Para atender à demanda, foram programados 1.089 ônibus extras, com possibilidade de reforço da frota.

Os destinos mais procurados são Rio de Janeiro, Florianópolis, Curitiba, Angra dos Reis e os litorais Norte e Sul de São Paulo.

A concessionária recomenda que os passageiros cheguem aos terminais com pelo menos uma hora de antecedência, levem documentos de identificação e consultem previamente a disponibilidade de passagens.

As unidades de atendimento de urgência e emergência da rede municipal permanecerão funcionando durante o feriado.

Entre os serviços com atendimento normal estão:

Assistências Médicas Ambulatoriais (AMAs);

AMAs/Unidades Básicas de Saúde (UBSs) Integradas.

Nas AMAs/UBSs Integradas, a parte correspondente à UBS funcionará exclusivamente para vacinação.

Outras unidades de saúde terão alterações no expediente.

Os parques municipais permanecerão abertos na sexta-feira (20), respeitando os horários de funcionamento de cada unidade.

O Elevado Presidente João Goulart, conhecido como Minhocão, ficará aberto exclusivamente para pedestres durante os três dias do feriado prolongado, de sexta-feira (20) a domingo (22), das 7h às 22h.

Já a Avenida Paulista e as vias da Liberdade serão destinadas exclusivamente a pedestres e ciclistas na sexta-feira (20) e no domingo (22), das 9h às 16h.

No sábado (21), não haverá a programação de ruas abertas nesses locais.

Os 63 Centros Educacionais Unificados (CEUs) da capital estarão abertos entre sexta-feira (20) e domingo (22), das 8h às 18h, com atividades para diferentes faixas etárias.

Os centros esportivos municipais também permanecerão abertos, seguindo os horários habituais de fins de semana e feriados.

Os mercados e sacolões municipais terão horários especiais na sexta-feira (20). Algumas unidades permanecerão fechadas.

Pinheiros: bancas das 8h às 14h e restaurantes até as 18h;

As centrais de abastecimento também terão horários diferenciados: a Central Leste funcionará das 7h às 13h, enquanto o Pátio do Pari abrirá das 3h às 16h.

Serviços municipais e atendimento ao público

Diversos serviços administrativos da Prefeitura de São Paulo não funcionarão na sexta-feira (20).

Praças de atendimento das subprefeituras;

Centros de Referência de Assistência Social (CRAS);

Centros de Referência Especializados de Assistência Social (CREAS);

Serviços presenciais de empregabilidade, empreendedorismo e agricultura;

Equipamentos municipais de atendimento à população imigrante e LGBTI.

O Centro de Atendimento da Fazenda retomará o expediente na segunda-feira (23), das 10h às 17h, mediante agendamento.

A unidade Descomplica SP 24 Horas reabrirá no sábado (21), às 6h.

Os serviços SP156, Empreenda Fácil e WiFi Livre SP terão funcionamento normal, segundo a prefeitura.

Os serviços essenciais de acolhimento e proteção social permanecerão funcionando durante o feriado.

Entre eles estão os centros de acolhida, os serviços especializados de abordagem social, a Central de Vagas e os serviços de acolhimento institucional para crianças e adolescentes.

A Casa da Mulher Brasileira e a Casa de Passagem Rosângela Rigo também funcionarão normalmente.

Já os Centros de Referência e Cidadania da Mulher (CRCM), Centros de Defesa e de Convivência da Mulher (CDCM) e postos avançados estarão fechados.

Os Conselhos Tutelares funcionarão em regime de plantão.

Os ecopontos municipais terão os seguintes horários:

Os pátios de compostagem permanecerão abertos das 6h às 22h.

Os equipamentos culturais administrados pela Prefeitura de São Paulo terão alterações no funcionamento entre sexta-feira (20) e domingo (22).

Os horários variam conforme o espaço, e a orientação é consultar a programação antes da visita.

articles.title: Como imagem sacra desaparecida há 40 anos foi recuperada em Caeté | G1
articles.standfirst: Escultura barroca do século XVIII foi identificada por um morador de Caeté, na Grande BH, após uma publicação nas redes sociais. Ministério Público recuperou peça.
articles.summary: A imagem sacra do século XVIII foi recuperada pelo Ministério Público e marca o início da restauração da Capela Nossa Senhora do Rosário, a mais antiga de Caeté.
articles.body:
imagem de Nossa Senhora do Rosário recuperada pelo MP — Foto: MPMG/Divulgação

Uma imagem sacra que ficou desaparecida por mais de 40 anos voltou ao altar da Capela Nossa Senhora do Rosário, em Caeté , na Região Metropolitana de Belo Horizonte, nesta semana.

A escultura, que data do século XVIII, foi recuperada pelo Ministério Público após ser identificada por um morador da cidade em uma publicação nas redes sociais ( entenda abaixo ).

Feita de madeira policromada e com 80 centímetros de altura, a peça é uma obra de arte em estilo barroco.

O retorno à capela foi marcado por uma celebração religiosa realizada na Igreja Matriz de Nossa Senhora do Bom Sucesso nesta quarta-feira (18).

Desde que desapareceu, na década de 1980, a peça estava registrada como procurada no Sistema de Resgate de Bens Culturais (Sondar) do Ministério Público.

Segundo a Arquidiocese de Belo Horizonte, a recuperação da escultura começou quando um morador de Caeté reconheceu a imagem em uma publicação nas redes sociais.

O homem guardava uma cópia de uma fotografia antiga da peça, desaparecida antes mesmo de ele nascer. Ao perceber a semelhança entre as imagens, procurou o Memorial da Arquidiocese, que acionou o MP.

A Coordenadoria das Promotorias de Justiça de Defesa do Patrimônio Cultural e Turístico de Minas Gerais (CPPC) passou a investigar o caso e solicitou um laudo para comparar a foto com a escultura divulgada na internet. Uma análise técnica confirmou que se tratava da imagem sacra que sumiu do acervo da Capela Nossa Senhora do Rosário.

Com a identificação, foram tomadas as providências para recuperar a peça.

O retorno da imagem também marcou uma nova etapa na preservação da Capela Nossa Senhora do Rosário, considerada o templo religioso mais antigo de Caeté e protegido pelo tombamento federal do Instituto do Patrimônio Histórico e Artístico Nacional (Iphan).

A Arquidiocese de Belo Horizonte e o Ministério Público anunciaram uma parceria para restaurar a igreja.

Os recursos serão destinados por meio da Plataforma Semente, do MP, que utiliza valores provenientes de medidas compensatórias ambientais para financiar projetos de interesse social.

O mecanismo também foi utilizado na reforma da Igreja Matriz de Nossa Senhora do Bom Sucesso, em 2025.

Construída em 1704, a Capela Nossa Senhora do Rosário é uma das principais referências históricas, religiosas e culturais de Caeté.

O templo foi erguido por Frei Simão de Santa Teresa, com a participação da Irmandade dos Homens Pretos, e representa um importante símbolo da religiosidade da população negra na cidade.

A igreja foi reaberta em 2025, após passar por intervenções emergenciais realizadas pela Arquidiocese de Belo Horizonte.

articles.title: Muslims poised to outnumber Christians globally by 2035 amid demographic shifts
articles.summary: Pew Research Center study projects Muslims will outnumber Christians worldwide by 2035, driven by higher fertility rates and younger populations.
articles.body: People practicing the Islamic faith are poised to outnumber Christians globally by 2035, becoming the world's largest religion, according to a new study released by the Pew Research Center. The detailed report attributes the shift primarily to higher fertility rates and younger populations among Muslims, who are growing at a faster rate than other major faiths. "Around the world, we find that Muslims tend to have more children than non-Muslims, [and] they tend to be younger as a result of having more children in the past," Pew senior demographer Conrad Hackett told Fox News Digital. WHY PEOPLE REALLY STOPPED HAVING KIDS: NEW STUDY UNCOVERS THE SURPRISING REASONS FAMILIES ARE SHRINKING Muslims have the highest fertility rate at 3.1 children per woman, followed by Christians at 2.5, according to the study. Between 2020 and 2025, Muslim women gave birth to 252 million babies, more than women of any other religion and compared to 208 million born to Christian mothers. If trends continue, the United States will also undergo a major religious shift. While Christians currently account for roughly 62% to 64% of U. S. adults, that share is expected to fall below 50% by 2065. POLL FINDS SHARP RISE IN YOUNG MEN CALLING RELIGION 'VERY IMPORTANT' By 2070, Christians are projected to make up less than half of the U. S. population, while religiously unaffiliated individuals, known as "nones," will rise to about 41%. "The Muslim population in the U. S. is growing faster than the Christian population, but Christians vastly outnumber Muslims in the U. S., and that's not going to change," Hackett said. By 2070, the Muslim population in the U. S. is expected to increase to nearly 4%, making Muslims the third-largest group in the country behind Christians and the religiously unaffiliated, surpassing the U.S. Jewish population. Globally, the demographic center of major faiths is also moving. By 2070, Pakistan is projected to have the largest Muslim population, followed by India, Nigeria and Indonesia, which currently has the largest Muslim population of any country. POPE LEO XIV TO VISIT FASTEST-GROWING CATHOLIC CONTINENT DURING 4-NATION AFRICA TRIP Meanwhile, the presence of Christianity is shifting southward. By 2070, more than half of the world's Christians will live in sub-Saharan Africa, and the Democratic Republic of the Congo is projected to surpass the U.S. as the country with the single greatest number of Christians. A century ago, most of the world's Christians lived in Europe, Hackett noted. However, Europe's population is now growing slowly and expected to shrink in the coming decades, while Africa's population expands rapidly. "Europe's population has been growing slowly, and Africa's population has been growing very quickly," Hackett said. "In the coming decades, Europe's population is expected to shrink, [while] Africa's population is going to expand a lot." Other religious demographics are shifting as well. The global Jewish population is expected to become increasingly concentrated, with 62% living in Israel by 2070, up from 46% in 2020. AGE OF FIRST-TIME MOTHERS HITS RECORD HIGH IN BLUE STATES AS BIRTH RATES KEEP FALLING In addition, the global Muslim population is projected to exceed 3.6 billion by 2070, compared to just under 3 billion Christians, according to Pew. Overall, Muslims and Christians are the only major religious groups projected to keep pace with the world's overall population growth, which is expected to increase by 29% between 2020 and 2070. Christians are projected to grow by 30% and Muslims by 80%. GEN Z FLOCKING TO CATHOLIC CHURCHES IN NYC FOR YOUTH GROUPS, SOCIAL EVENTS AMID CONVERSION BOOM Beyond organized religions, many countries continue to see a surge in "nones," those with no religious affiliation, atheists or agnostics. While China holds a massive proportion of the world's religiously unaffiliated, its population decline will offset growth elsewhere, Hackett said. Excluding China, the global population of "nones" is projected to grow by more than 180 million by 2070. The Associated Press contributed to this report.

articles.title: Wife and daughter arrested after DNA IDs man whose severed head was found in trash bag
articles.summary: Mary Fitzmaurice allegedly kept collecting her father's Social Security and pension benefits after his death, telling relatives he was still alive.
articles.body: A California woman and her daughter were arrested more than four years after a woman walking her dog found a man's severed head in a trash bag, authorities said. The Placer County Sheriff’s Office identified the man as Paul Wesley Fitzmaurice Jr., 73, who had never been reported missing. Authorities said his wife and daughter had told relatives the victim was still alive. His daughter, 45-year-old Mary Fitzmaurice, and his wife, 75-year-old Georgia "Gwenn" Fitzmaurice, were booked into the South Placer Jail on Tuesday, officials said in a news release. Mary was booked on suspicion of murder and Gwenn on suspicion of being an accessory. DNA BREAKTHROUGH LEADS TO ARREST IN GRISLY 33-YEAR-OLD COLD CASE INVESTIGATORS NEVER GAVE UP ON The women "kept up the facade to family and friends that Paul was still alive," Placer County Sheriff Wayne Woo said at a news conference Wednesday. He said they continued receiving Fitzmaurice’s Social Security benefits and California public pension after his death. Woo said the women told some of Fitzmaurice’s estranged relatives "he was being a recluse, and he would disappear for days at a time." They claimed he "would come back to the house every week or so and stay for a couple of days," Woo said. In its news release, the sheriff’s office alleged Mary killed her father and the two women "conspired to dispose of his remains." At Wednesday’s news conference, Placer County District Attorney Morgan Gire said prosecutors expected to file a murder charge against Mary Fitzmaurice by the end of the day and were weighing additional charges related to the killing and the collection of Fitzmaurice’s benefits. Asked whether money was a motive, Woo said, "There’s still a lot of investigative work to be done, and I would be speculating on motive at this point." NEW CALIFORNIA LAW EXPANDS DNA TOOLS FOR MISSING PERSONS INVESTIGATIONS The dog walker found the bag on Sept. 28, 2022, in the Todd Valley area of Foresthill while the Mosquito Fire was burning nearby. Woo said the discovery drew little attention at the time. "The people that didn’t forget about this case is the residents of Foresthill and our cold case detectives," Woo said. The remains were too decomposed for investigators to identify the man. Forensic experts at California State University, Chico, helped produce an artist’s rendering, but it yielded no match in missing-person cases. A search of the national law enforcement DNA database also came up empty. In January 2024, detectives sent a DNA sample to Othram Labs, which used forensic genetic genealogy to find possible distant relatives. With the FBI’s help, investigators traced the family tree and obtained a DNA sample from an out-of-state relative that helped confirm Fitzmaurice’s identity. GIRL KNOWN AS 'CHELSEA JANE DOE' ID'D 26 YEARS AFTER MUTILATED BODY FOUND HUNDREDS OF MILES FROM HOME STATE Othram said in a news release that Fitzmaurice’s identification marked the 94th publicly announced case in California in which investigators used its technology to identify someone. The sheriff’s office said in its release that investigators believe Mary killed her father at the family’s Citrus Heights home, which detectives searched Tuesday with help from the FBI. When asked at the briefing where Fitzmaurice was killed, Woo said, "With evidence that we gathered and collected yesterday, we’ll hopefully determine that." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Woo said the rest of Fitzmaurice’s remains have yet to be found. "We did not find any remains at the residence yesterday," he said.

articles.title: Kenya’s milk shortage deepens as drought hits farmers and pushes up prices
articles.summary: Farmers are receiving higher payments but are producing far less milk and also face rising prices for hay.
articles.body:
Nairobi, Kenya – Milk is becoming harder to find in parts of Kenya as prolonged dry conditions take a toll on dairy farmers, disrupting supplies to major towns and pushing up prices.

In Nairobi, some popular brands have become increasingly difficult to find in shops. A 500ml (1-pint) packet of Tuzo, Dairy Best or Mt Kenya milk sells for 79 to 89 Kenyan shillings ($0.61 to $0.68), but supplies have been limited. New brands have appeared on supermarket shelves at about 65 shillings ($0.50) while some neighbourhood shops visited by Al Jazeera were charging as much as 100 shillings ($0.77) for the same quantity.

The shortage is being felt across the dairy supply chain, from farmers struggling to feed their animals to businesses that depend on a steady supply of fresh milk.

In Kajiado County, southwest of Nairobi, dairy farmers said a prolonged dry spell has sharply reduced milk production over the past three months.

Jennifer Leshinka, a farmer in Bisil, told Al Jazeera that her daily milk production had fallen from 120 litres (32 gallons) to 50 litres (13 gallons). With natural pasture dwindling, she has had to buy hay to feed her animals. Some of her dairy animals have also been moved to neighbouring counties in search of grazing land.

“I supplement the little natural grass with several bales of hay to feed my animals, which has become expensive. A bale of hay is currently retailing between 100 and 150 shillings [$0.77 to $1.15], yet it cannot sustain a mature animal for a day,” Leshinka said.

The pressure is not limited to Kajiado. Diminishing pasture and water supplies are affecting pastoralists in arid and semiarid areas as well as dairy farmers in the highlands, another important milk-producing region.

Jackson Sinkeet, a farmer who supplies raw milk to hotels across the Nairobi metropolitan area, said falling yields have made it difficult to meet orders, even from customers willing to pay higher prices.

He warned that the situation could worsen if dry conditions persist.

Cooperatives and businesses feel the shortage

The decline in production is also affecting dairy cooperatives, which collect milk from farmers and supply major processors.

Jeremiah Ole Ncharo, Kajiado County’s executive committee member in charge of cooperatives, told Al Jazeera that at least five major women-led dairy cooperatives have reported a 50 percent drop in milk deliveries from their members during the dry period.

He said the reduced volumes were affecting supplies to large milk processors, adding to pressure on the formal market.

In Nairobi, hotelier Joram Kamau said businesses were spending hours queuing at major processors’ depots to obtain rationed milk.

The shortage has also raised concerns about the products available in the market. Kamau said he was worried about the growing presence of powdered milk products whose quality and authenticity he questioned. He said he would rather wait for genuine milk, even if it cost more, than risk buying questionable products and losing customers.

Government outlines response as milk supplies fall

Agriculture Cabinet Secretary Mutahi Kagwe told Al Jazeera that the current shortage was largely linked to prolonged dry conditions, which have reduced the availability of pasture, fodder and water, affecting animal productivity and the amount of milk delivered to processors.

He said Kenya’s dairy industry has continued to grow with national milk production rising from 4.64 billion kilogrammes (10.23 billion pounds) in 2021 to 5.52 billion kilogrammes (12.17 billion pounds) in 2025. Formal milk deliveries also increased from about 802 million litres (212 million gallons) to 1.01 billion litres (267 million gallons) over the same period.

However, more recent figures point to a decline in milk reaching formal processors. Kagwe said monthly deliveries averaged about 83.45 million litres (22 million gallons) in 2025, compared with 74.09 million litres (19.57 million gallons) in September.

He said the decline has affected volumes available for processing, particularly UHT milk, which has a longer shelf life and helps maintain supplies.

However, government market surveillance for the week ending October 30 indicated a slight improvement in UHT milk availability across most parts of the country. Other dairy products, including fermented milk, butter and cheese, were generally available at normal stock levels.

Kagwe said the government was monitoring production, processor stocks, producer prices and retail prices. It was also facilitating regional transfers of milk and dairy products, particularly within the East African Community, while encouraging processors to collect more milk from farmers and cooperatives.

He added that farmers were receiving better prices amid tighter supplies. The average gross producer price rose to about 53.88 shillings ($0.41) per litre (1 quart) in July, compared with an average of 49.58 shillings ($0.38) in 2025.

Buffalo proposal offers no immediate relief

To address longer-term challenges in the dairy sector, the government is looking at ways to increase production and improve farmers’ resilience.

Kagwe said planned measures included expanding fodder production and conservation, continuing a subsidised artificial insemination programme to improve dairy genetics and distributing milk coolers to organised farmer groups. The restructuring of the state-owned dairy processor New KCC is also expected to improve services to producers and consumers.

The government is also exploring President William Ruto’s proposal to introduce Indian water buffaloes to Kenya as an additional source of milk.

Kagwe told Al Jazeera that the initiative was still at an early stage. Kenya would first need to establish veterinary and import requirements, identify suitable breeds and sources, and bring in a limited number of animals to assess their adaptability and productivity under local conditions.

India, the world’s largest milk producer, relies on buffaloes for about 43 percent of its milk production. Buffalo milk has a relatively high fat and solids content, making it suitable for products such as cheese and butter.

But Kagwe said the proposal should be seen as a medium- to long-term opportunity rather than a response to the current shortage.

For farmers such as Leshinka and Sinkeet, the immediate challenge remains the rising cost of keeping their animals fed and productive. In Nairobi, businesses are still struggling to secure enough milk to meet customer demand.

“The animals’ milk yield has dropped significantly. I am unable to supply my customers, who are willing to pay higher prices, because the milk is simply not available,” Sinkeet told Al Jazeera.

articles.title: Van Gogh painting sells for $190.4m after row over Nazi history
articles.summary: Châtaigniers en fleurs was painted in 1890 in the final two months of Vincent van Gogh's life.
articles.body:
Auction house Sotheby's has sold a painting by Vincent van Gogh for a record $190.4m (£144.8m).

The sale of Châtaigniers en fleurs ("Chestnut Trees in Blossom") shatters the renowned artist's previous auction record of $117.2 million set in 2022.

The historic sale in New York on Wednesday comes after an eleventh-hour agreement was reached to resolve a dispute regarding claims the art piece was previously sold under duress during the rise of the Nazis.

Châtaigniers en fleurs was painted in 1890 in the final two months of Van Gogh's life. It is considered one of the most important works of art from that period to remain in private hands, according to Sotheby's.

Sotheby's auction of $180m Van Gogh challenged over claims it was 'sold under duress'

It was not immediately clear who purchased the painting. The BBC has contacted Sotheby's for comment.

The oil painting, which was estimated to carry a value of $180m (£136m) prior to the sale, was put up for auction as part of a set called the Blaquier-Arrieta Collection.

Sotheby's announced in the hours before the auction that it had resolved a dispute between the Blaquier-Arrieta family and the heirs of the Fischer family - the prior German owners of the work - regarding the sale.

Representatives acting for heirs of the Fischer family had claimed the painting may have been sold under duress during the rise of the Nazis.

A lawyer for the family's heirs reportedly wrote to Sotheby's on their behalf, telling the auction house that the painting was sold in Amsterdam before World War Two because of financial losses the Fischer family's publishing company suffered under the Nazis. The BBC has contacted the lawyer for comment.

"In recognition of the painting's complex Nazi-era history and the suffering endured by the Fischer family during the Holocaust, the two families have reached a mutually satisfactory resolution and the work will be sold pursuant to their agreement," Sotheby's said on Wednesday.

Sotheby's website details the provenance of the oil painting and how it has researched the artwork changing hands since 1890.

It says Samuel Fischer - a famous German publisher - acquired it 1909 before it was passed down in his family after his death in 1934.

The painting was deposited with Paul Cassirer in Amsterdam in 1932 or 1933 before it went to Henriette and Marcel Kapferer in Paris in 1936, Sotheby's said.

Four other owners then had the painting.

The Blaquier family acquired it in 1975 and owned it for more than half a century before the latest sale, the auction house said.

articles.title: After clip shows MP cops threatening couple, CM suspends additional SP, 5 cops
articles.summary: BHOPAL: Taking cognisance of a viral hotel video in Madhya Pradesh's Seoni district, purportedly showing senior police officers harassing an adult couple
articles.body: BHOPAL: Taking cognisance of a viral hotel video in Madhya Pradesh's Seoni district, purportedly showing senior police officers harassing an adult couple and threatening to plant narcotics in the man's belongings to frame him in a drugs case, chief minister Mohan Yadav on Wednesday ordered the suspension of additional SP Deepak Mishra, SDOP Chanchalesh Markam, Kotwali police station in-charge Satish Tiwari and three other police personnel.The CM also directed a detailed and impartial inquiry into the episode, to be conducted by the deputy inspector general of police, Chhindwara range, before submitting a report.The purported footage from the Seoni hotel on Tuesday captured additional SP Mishra telling his staff to put ganja (cannabis) in the man's bag.The video also appeared to show uniformed personnel questioning and intimidating the couple, raising serious questions about police conduct and intrusion into the private lives of consenting adults.'Why are cops interfering in private matters?' According to a statement issued after the CM's intervention, the video showed police personnel speaking to a woman and a man inside a hotel room in an objectionable and inappropriate manner, while threatening to place narcotic substances among their belongings.Apart from Mishra, Markam and Satish Tiwari, head constable Naveen Tiwari, constable and driver Krishna Parte and constable Salman Khan, who is posted with the 8th Battalion of the Special Armed Force in Chhindwara, were also placed under suspension in connection with the incident.Further action will be decided on the findings of the inquiry report to be submitted by the DIG, Chhindwara range.Meanwhile, the episode put the govt in the line of Opposition fire, as the Congress questioned the conduct of the police while demanding accountability of the home department, which is headed by the CM. articles.title: Why a trio of experts alleges Jeffrey Epstein did not die by suicide
articles.summary: A new report alleges that injuries on Epstein’s body were overlooked by medical examiners during his 2019 autopsy.
articles.body:
A trio of experts has released a report casting doubt on whether convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein died by suicide in his jail cell in 2019, as a medical examiner in the United States previously ruled.

In documents obtained by Al Jazeera and other media outlets, Michael Freeman, Anders Eriksson and Itiel Dror – a forensic scientist, a forensic pathologist and a cognitive scientist – said the injuries on Epstein’s body were “most consistent with homicidal strangulation”, not suicide.

“The pattern, distribution, and multitude of injuries are not explained by a suicidal hanging,” their report reads.

Instead, they suggest Epstein was first assaulted and then strangled, providing an alternative narrative to the medical examiner’s 2019 report.

The cause of Epstein’s death has long been a source of controversy and conspiracy theories.

A wealthy businessman, Epstein cultivated a range of high-profile relationships with leaders in politics, industry, academia and the arts. His network of contacts included US presidents Bill Clinton and Donald Trump.

Those connections have raised questions about whether there was a cover-up of Epstein’s crimes – or whether some of his associates knowingly turned a blind eye.

In 2008, Epstein pleaded guilty to the solicitation of a minor for sex as part of a plea deal that saw him serve 13 months behind bars. Later, in 2019, he was arrested on federal charges of sex trafficking, with prosecutors accusing him of having “sexually exploited and abused dozens of underage girls”.

He died in a New York City jail while awaiting trial.

Medical examiner Kristin Roman performed the autopsy on Epstein’s body. She and New York City’s Chief Medical Examiner Barbara Sampson ultimately ruled that the evidence pointed to a suicide by hanging.

Other experts have sided with their ruling, pointing out that, while the circumstances of Epstein’s death were unusual, they are not necessarily inconsistent with suicide.

But Epstein’s brother, Mark, has long doubted the medical examiner’s findings. He gave Freeman, an Oregon-based forensic scientist, access to the death records.

Freeman has consulted in trials where families have questioned the narratives put forward by law enforcement about how someone died, including in high-profile cases like the murder of George Floyd.

Eriksson, meanwhile, is a Sweden-based forensic pathologist who has researched issues like shaken baby syndrome, a controversial diagnosis used to prosecute some adults for abuse of young children.

He and Freeman worked alongside Dror, a cognitive scientist who studies biases in forensic science.

At the time of his death, Epstein was a well-known figure, and Dror said the investigators handling his case would have been subject to significant political pressure.

“It’s so obvious this played a critical role in the examination of the body,” Dror told Al Jazeera.

“There was at stake a lot of emotion, a lot of people involved, a lot of politics involved, so many factors. You can list them for an hour, and all of those interfered and biased and influenced what should be a scientific decision.”

Dror explained that he and his colleagues pored over photos and records related to Epstein’s death and concluded that the medical examiner had wrongly ruled it a suicide.

In their report, the trio noted a number of issues with the initial investigation.

The prison personnel who found Epstein’s body did not take any photos before moving it, for instance. Investigators also failed to identify the ligature, the object that was actually around Epstein’s neck, they said.

They allege that some avenues of investigation went unexplored. The prison guard who first came across Epstein’s body initially refused to be interviewed, according to the report, and the medical examiner who determined the case was a suicide was not allowed to visit the prison.

The report also disagrees with the medical examiner’s assessment of Epstein’s injuries.

Marks left by the ligature on Epstein’s neck, the researchers said, were not slanted in the way that would be expected if his body had been hanging from the bedpost in his cell.

They observed bruising on Epstein’s back, shoulder and neck that they said was not acknowledged in the medical examiner’s original statements.

Those injuries, their report said, are “most consistent with homicidal strangulation from behind, most likely using a narrow knotted fabric ligature”.

Freeman, Eriksson and Dror believe either that the prison guard who found Epstein was lying about finding his body hanging in the cell, or that the body was deliberately put into that position to make it seem like a suicide had taken place.

articles.title: In 1970s, Dawood Ibrahim lived here with family before his rise in Mumbai's underworld; now, 87-year-old building faces demolition
articles.summary: MUMBAI: The BMC is likely to begin demolishing the 87-year-old Haji Ismail Haji Habib Musafirkhana on Thursday.
articles.body: MUMBAI: The BMC is likely to begin demolishing the 87-year-old Haji Ismail Haji Habib Musafirkhana on Thursday. The building was once home to the family of underworld don Dawood Ibrahim. BMC had scheduled the demolition for Nov 18 and 19. But work did not begin on Wednesday.A civic notice said BMC received a letter from Saifee Burhani Upliftment Trust (SBUT) on the building's dilapidated and dangerous condition, requesting BMC to evict its occupants and demolish the structure in accordance with a Bombay High Court order of Aug 2020. In clarification issued on Oct 23 this year, SBUT stated the building falls under Sector 8 of its cluster redevelopment scheme, with a portion of it lying within the alignment of a proposed road.An officer said police were ready to provide protection and would proceed to the site whenever BMC called them.Constructed in 1939, the ground-plus-one-storey building has 36 rooms and was initially used as temporary accommodation for Haj pilgrims. It was later categorised as a C-1 structure, indicating it was dilapidated. A demolition notice was then issued.The civic notice stated an internal road was under construction and the C-1 structure fell within its alignment, obstructing the widening of the Second Cooper Street layout road. The occupant of the ground-floor prayer hall was asked to move to alternative accommodation offered by SBUT. During a recent site inspection, BMC found the building had been vacated, except for the ground floor (used as a prayer hall).In the early 1970s, police constable Ibrahim Kaskar, his wife Amina Bi and their children moved from Temkar Mohalla to a room in Musafirkhana.One of their children, Dawood Ibrahim, took to crime and emerged as a major threat to rival gangs. He allegedly occupied space on the ground floor, near the building's entrance, where he would sit with friends and gang members.Dawood fled Mumbai in 1986. The building had more than two dozen tenants. A lane away stood Damarwala Building, where Dawood's younger brother, Iqbal Kaskar, stayed after his release from Arthur Road Jail in 2007. Kaskar had been deported from UAE in 2003 along with a dozen other members of the Dawood gang.The SBUT, which is undertaking a cluster redevelopment project in Bhendi Bazar, acquired six rooms in Damarwala Building through a public auction conducted by the Smugglers and Foreign Exchange Manipulators (Forfeiture of Property) Act (SAFEMA) authorities.The rooms were allegedly owned by Kaskar and Dawood's relatives. Hotel Raunaq Afroz, also known as Delhi Zaika, near Damarwala Building, was also acquired by SBUT through an auction. articles.title: Mamdani grilled on rhetoric toward Oct 7, combating antisemitism as Jewish New Yorkers fear current climate
articles.summary: New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani defended his Oct. 7 X post at The New York Times' DealBook Summit, telling Andrew Ross Sorkin there must be room to mourn everyone.
articles.body: New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani was grilled Wednesday on his efforts to combat antisemitism during his appearance at The New York Times DealBook Summit. After greeting his "comrades" at the beginning of his sit-down, Mamdani was pressed by The New York Times' Andrew Ross Sorkin about the importance of "language," specifically in relation to the Jewish community in New York City and growing antisemitism. Sorkin pointed to Mamdani's controversial X post commemorating the Oct. 7 terrorist attack committed against Israel, which dedicated more words toward the plight of the Palestinians and Israel's military response in Gaza than the roughly 1,200 Israelis who were brutally murdered that day by Hamas. BILL MAHER MOCKS MAMDANI FOR PIVOTING TO ISRAEL CRITICISM IN OCT 7 TRIBUTE, CALLS IT 'TONE-DEAF' "The head of the Reform Jewish movement (had) said at the time that they thought that the statement made New Yorkers less safe. And then there was a rabbi who said — they called himself a fan of yours — he said, 'Can we just have one day?'" Sorkin told Mamdani. "And I'm curious, again, about the language you use. And the reason I mention it is, you know, 53%, I think, of hate crimes in New York City are against Jews. "And, so, when you use language in this regard — and I know we can have a whole debate about whether condemning Israel gets conflated with antisemitism and this and that — but do you feel like there's an extra sort of responsibility or distinction in the language you use when you use it?" Mamdani pushed back at the premise of the question, saying his X post "doesn't cover the entirety of the day," which included a vigil honoring the Oct. 7 victims, noting that he was also protested for attending the vigil. "My politics is one that believes that there has to be room to mourn everyone," Mamdani said. "And what I sought to do not only in the statement, but also in my physical attendance at that vigil, which I had attended the year before, was to make clear that I will oppose with every bone in my body the violations of international law, no matter who commits them, who conducts them. And that's why I've called Oct. 7 a war crime. And that is why I have also been immensely critical of the Israeli government as well." MAMDANI DINED AT NYC RESTAURANT LINKED TO ANTI-ISRAEL MENU AFTER BEING BOOED AT OCT 7 VIGIL: REPORT The democratic socialist mayor slammed the "objectionable" statistic that Jewish New Yorkers are the victims of more than half of all hate crimes despite being 10-12% of the city's population. "That, to me, is unacceptable, because in addition to being proud of being the mayor of New York City, I'm also proud to be the mayor of the most Jewish city in the United States of America," Mamdani told Sorkin. "So much of what so many of us love about New York is tied up in that same legacy. And to me, the responsibility is you have to root out antisemitism. You have to root out any form of bigotry. "And that there will be, and there are, Jewish New Yorkers, as well as New Yorkers of other faiths or no faiths at all, who disagree with me on my views on Israel and Palestine," the mayor continued. "There's no question. My job is to still deliver for them as well, and to deliver them the best possible city, because, at the end of the day, they live in the same city." "I get it," Sorkin interjected. "My question is, would you ever think about sending out one tweet on Oct. 7, saying how terrible what happened on Oct. 7 was, and then waiting till Oct. 8 to say how terrible you think Israel has handled the situation?" Sorkin's follow-up question sparked applause from the audience. "My point being, this is a day that is not only a horrific war crime. It is also a day that has been used as a justification for all that followed it. And it is in that day that it is important, like in any day, to mourn the totality of its impact." Mamdani insisted he understands "the other side" of the argument but doubled down on his stance. I speak about the importance of extending these same values, of empathy. And that is who I am," he added.

articles.title: Leasehold system set to be scrapped in England and Wales
articles.summary: The proposed Commonhold and Leasehold Reform Bill will also include capping ground rent at £250.
articles.body:
The government is to introduce new laws to scrap the ownership rules for flats in England and Wales and cap ground rents at £250 a year.

Under the plans, which will not become law until at least next year, most new leasehold flats will eventually be banned and replaced with commonhold, where residents collectively own and manage their buildings.

Housing Minister Matthew Pennycook said the current leasehold system was "blighting lives" and was an "anachronism in the 21st century".

But the Residential Freehold Association says the plan is an "unprecedented abuse" of their rights, which will wipe billions from the value of pension funds, which have invested heavily in property.

The Commonhold and Leasehold Reform Bill, to be published on Thursday, is likely to contain further details on when the measures would come into force.

In order to become law, the bill would first need to be approved by both Houses of Parliament, a process that will take several months.

The bill will also include plans to cap ground rent - the annual fee paid by current leaseholders to their freeholder - at £250 from 2028. That will then be reduced to a "peppercorn" rate - which is effectively nothing - after 40 years.

Fozia Malik lives in a one-bedroom flat in Oldham and says her ground rent will go up from £150 to £300 in January. That is alongside service charges of more than £4,000 a year.

Malik says her block of flats has been plagued by a number of problems, including fire safety issues and rising costs.

The managing agent for her building says the service charges are due to costs that are out of its control and high insurance because of fire safety issues.

But Malik says she would "never" buy a leasehold flat again, describing it as a "continuous torture cell".

When she bought her flat, Malik assumed the system would work in the same way it does in Pakistan, where she grew up, and in most other countries, where buying a home also means owning a share of the land it sits on.

However, in England, most flats are sold on a leasehold basis. That gives the buyer the right to occupy and use a property for a set period of time, but the freeholder retains ultimate ownership of the building and the land.

Systems based on shared ownership and collective management - such as commonhold - are already standard in many parts of the world, including Australia, New Zealand, the US, Canada and much of continental Europe. They give residents ownership of their home and a stake in the building's common areas.

Scotland does not have leasehold tenures, while Northern Ireland has just a handful of leasehold properties.

The government says its reforms are intended to bring England and Wales more closely in line with other other countries around the world, which do not have leaseholds.

It comes as more than 1,000 leaseholders have contacted the BBC over the past two years with complaints about the current system.

Campaigners have welcomed many of the reforms, but questioned what happens to the millions of people who already own leasehold homes.

While the legislation is expected to reshape ownership for new developments, converting existing leasehold buildings into commonhold is far more complicated. And it has led to concerns that current leaseholders will be left behind.

Giles Grover, from the campaign group End Our Cladding Scandal, says there is a risk the proposed changes will create a two-tier system of those buying new homes and existing leaseholders.

He began campaigning on behalf of flat owners following the Grenfell Tower tragedy. He says: "It's so complicated, will the measures that are being introduced actually benefit everyone?"

The government says the bill will make it easier for existing leaseholders to convert to commonhold, abolish forfeiture - so people cannot lose their homes over relatively small debts - improve transparency around service charges and crack down on estate charges.

Pennycook says it will transform "the experience of homeownership for existing leaseholders by giving them greater rights and protections and providing them with easy and effective escape routes".

However, the issue about how existing leaseholders can move into commonhold and how freeholders should be compensated remains unresolved.

A spokesperson for the Residential Freehold Association, which represents the UK's largest freeholders, says £18.7bn "could be wiped out from investments overnight".

The association says property investors, which often include pension funds, have invested £15bn in residential ground rents.

articles.body: SAN JUAN, Puerto Rico — Salvadoran President Nayib Bukele said Wednesday that his troops demolished the lavish home of a prominent gang leader in Haiti known as Jeff. It wasn’t immediately clear if he was killed. Bukele posted a video on X that depicts an old video of Jeff posing in front of his mansion in the Caribbean country and then cuts to Salvadoran helicopters flying toward it as they fire shot after shot, with big plumes of smoke rising from Jeff’s home. “My gift to the Haitian people on the anniversary of the Battle of Vertières,” Bukele wrote. The 1803 battle was critical in helping secure Haiti’s independence from France and transforming it into the world’s first Black republic. It wasn’t immediately known if Haiti’s police and army were involved. A U.N.-backed gang suppression force said that it wasn’t involved. Hours after the announcement, thousands of Haitians marched through the streets of Port-au-Prince and beyond for the second consecutive day in praise of El Salvador’s leader as they chanted, “Bukele! Bukele!” Among those celebrating Wednesday’s attack was Mario Jean-Pierre, a 45-year-old salesperson in Port-au-Prince. “Jeff is a criminal and I hope he died,” he said. “We asked for help; Bukele answered us.” Gang leader flaunted pool visible by satellite Jeff is considered one of Haiti’s most powerful gang leaders. His real name is Jeff Larose, but he’s known as Jeff Canaan, Jeff Gwo Lwa and Taliban. His so-called Taliban gang, which has a couple hundred members, has long controlled a community known as Canaan in northern Port-au-Prince. “It is one of the most organized gangs, with the strictest territorial control,” said Diego Da Rin, a Haiti expert with International Crisis Group. Da Rin said the attack on Jeff’s home was the obvious next step for Bukele’s operations. Jeff built the home in mid-2024, complete with a pool emblazoned with his logo. “It’s very easy to identify it by satellite,” Da Rin said. “It was a very defiant act by him.” He noted that Jeff’s home was very vulnerable to an aerial attack, but it was built in a place where attacking it by land would have been extremely difficult. Da Rin said Jeff was among a handful of gang leaders who have built mansions in recent years. “In a way, they felt untouchable in their territory,” he said. The use of explosive drones and helicopters, which Haitian police and military lack, has changed that. While it has allowed forces to chase after gangs more efficiently, it also has multiplied the number of innocent victims and prompted gangs to retaliate against civilians. “It is not surprising that gangs would seek to undermine enthusiasm for the arrival of new forces by targeting civilians who have expressed support for security operations,” said Sandra Pellegrini, a senior analyst with Armed Conflict Location and Event Data. She and Da Rin warned that despite Bukele’s attacks against Haitian gangs, one persistent challenge is forces retaining long-term control over territories recaptured from gangs, further placing civilians at risk. Two powerful ‘warlords’ under attack Da Rin said he doubts Jeff was staying at the mansion when it was attacked early Wednesday given that on Nov. 8, Salvadoran troops attacked the home of Wilson Joseph, best known as Lanmò San Jou and leader of the 400 Mawozo gang. He wasn’t killed in the attack. Da Rin said gang leaders have several residences and can always seek shelter in any home within the territory they control. He noted that Jeff and Lanmò San Jou are allies and control the main roads north and east of Port-au-Prince that lead to other cities and towns, charging tolls that have become their main source of revenue. “He and Lanmò San Jou are arguably the most powerful warlords in Port-au-Prince,” Da Rin said. Jeff operates in Canaan, which was established as an informal community after a devastating earthquake hit Haiti in January 2010. Tens of thousands of people are estimated to now live there. Last month, Bukele deployed around 2,500 troops to Haiti after four of their own came under attack on Oct. 18 while deep in gang territory. They remain missing.

articles.title: Trump pushes for three-way nuclear deal as Russia and China show little interest
articles.summary: President Donald Trump has repeatedly placed nonproliferation near the top of the agenda for his unprecedented trilateral meeting Thursday with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin, but his counterparts have expressed little interest in committing to new limitations on their nuclear arsenals.
articles.body: WASHINGTON — President Donald Trump has repeatedly placed nonproliferation near the top of the agenda for his trilateral meeting Thursday with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin, although his counterparts have expressed little interest in committing to new limitations on their nuclear arsenals. Trump has been pushing for China to join the U.S. and Russia in a new nuclear arms control agreement since his first term in office. Still, he has sought to limit expectations for any major progress in Shenzhen, China, where the world’s top three nuclear powers are meeting on the sidelines of a summit of Asia-Pacific leaders. Russia suspended its participation in New START, its last remaining nuclear arms pact with the U.S., when it invaded Ukraine in 2022, denying inspections of its nuclear sites. Ahead of the treaty’s expiration this past February, Russia said it would keep to the deal’s limitations on its arsenal for another year, but Trump insisted a new agreement must include China and possibly other nuclear powers. China has said an arms control agreement should remain between the U.S. and Russia, which together hold nearly 90% of the world’s nuclear arsenal with more than 5,000 warheads each. China has about 600, according to Pentagon estimates, though by 2030 it could have up to 1,000 if its arsenal continues to expand at the current rate. “China is building up its nuclear arsenal to a very significant degree, and it will continue to do so, and wants to continue to do so,” David Sacks, a senior fellow for Asia studies at the Council on Foreign Relations, told reporters Wednesday. The Chinese foreign ministry has declined to say whether nuclear arms control will be discussed at the trilateral meeting on Thursday, with spokesperson Mao Ning saying earlier this week that the three leaders “will have an in-depth exchange of views on important issues bearing on global peace.” In a call last week, Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi “agreed on the importance of meaningful leader-level conversations to advance goals such as peace and denuclearization,” according to a U.S. readout of the call. The Chinese readout made no reference to such a discussion. Trump has admitted that it will be difficult to get Russia and China to consider reducing their nuclear arsenals. “So we’re going to talk about denuclearization. Tough subject because it’s very hard for any of us to say we’ll get rid of our nukes, right? But especially since you do have other countries,” he said Monday. “But we’re going to be talking about denuclearization.” Even in the hours leading up to this week’s Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen, the world’s top two nuclear powers were making shows of force. On Tuesday, the U.S. launched an unarmed intercontinental ballistic missile in a previously unannounced test at Vandenberg Space Force Base in California. Hours later, Russia landed two strategic bombers in Vietnam to coincide with Putin’s arrival in China. While one meeting is not likely to produce dramatic breakthroughs, it could kickstart a process that leads to sustained, formal bilateral or multilateral negotiations on nuclear risk reduction, arms control and disarmament, said Daryl Kimball, executive director of the Washington-based Arms Control Association. “A top priority for all three leaders should be to head off a costly, escalatory nuclear arms race involving the further buildup of nuclear forces and the resumption of nuclear testing by any state,” he said. Da Wei, director of the Center for International Security and Strategy at Tsinghua University in Beijing, said nuclear arms control was not a “proper topic” for the trilateral meeting given the complexity of the issue and how little time Trump, Putin and Xi will have together. But if the three leaders “can say something about nuclear stability, like a nuclear war is not winnable and should not be fought, I think that will be helpful,” he said in an interview Wednesday. Rubio has acknowledged that a new agreement could take some time. “Past agreements, including New START, took years to negotiate and were built upon decades of precedent. They were also between two powers, not three or more,” he wrote on Substack in February. “However, just because something is hard does not mean we should not pursue it or settle for less.”

articles.title: China's Xi Jinping has orchestrated a  remarkable diplomatic moment - but it comes with pitfalls
articles.summary: The meeting comes with challenges as there are things Xi does not appear keen to discuss with Putin and Trump.
articles.body:
Xi Jinping will believe he has achieved something no other world leader could in securing a historic summit with Vladimir Putin and Donald Trump in Shenzhen.

For decades, Washington and its western allies shaped the world order.

Yet it is China that has orchestrated the remarkable diplomatic spectacle of three of the world's most powerful protagonists sitting around the table.

And surrounding it all is the futuristic display that is Shenzhen, with driverless cars cruising past as drones fly overhead and robots - literally - dance in the streets.

Ostensibly, this is an economic summit for Asia Pacific leaders. But for Xi, it is also a demonstration of China's grip on the global economy and world politics.

His country is no longer just reacting to decisions made in Washington, London or Brussels - instead Beijing is at the heart of conversations which are reshaping the international order.

But this meeting is not without its pitfalls for Xi as there are many things he does not appear keen to discuss with Putin and Trump.

Follow live updates: Trump, Xi and Putin hold historic meeting on Apec sidelines

First, China is not keen for the war in Ukraine, now well into its fifth year, to be on the agenda.

This is a delicate balancing act for Xi who is aware his relationship with Putin may damage China's connections in Europe. The EU is a key market, especially now when the Chinese economy is heavily relying on exports.

However Xi also doesn't want the war to end in a way that will destabilise Russia, a key ally and neighbour.

Beijing is still trying to maintain that it is neutral in this war and has repeatedly called for negotiations and a political settlement while avoiding condemnation of Russia's full-scale invasion.

The US, especially under the previous Biden administration, and Europe have accused China of sending Russia components that it could use in its war in Ukraine, while also propping up the country's economy by buying oil and gas.

Xi wants to keep Putin close, but not too close because he also doesn't want Russia's problems to become China's problems.

Donald Trump has already made it clear he wants the three leaders to discuss limiting the world's supply of nuclear weapons.

The US and Russia possess the world's largest stockpile of nuclear warheads. But China is rapidly expanding its own arsenal, which is raising alarm bells in Washington.

The last major US-Russian arms control treaty, known as New START, expired in February this year, triggering fears of an arms race. The agreement had set a cap to control the number of nuclear weapons in US and Russia's arsenal.

Trump would like China to be included in any new agreement, but Beijing has pushed back.

Xi's argument will be that his arsenal is considerably smaller than what Washington and Moscow own, and, therefore, it would be unfair for Beijing to be bound by their limits. China also believes it should have the freedom to develop its own nuclear capabilities.

This subject could complicate Xi's bid for China to be recognised as a leader on the world stage - because the US could argue that the status includes being a responsible nuclear power.

Xi will want to control the optics of this meeting, from start to finish.

Chinese officials like to nail down agendas with talking points and produce carefully choreographed speeches.

But in this unprecedented summit, Xi will have to live with two very unpredictable leaders.

Both Trump and Putin have their own agendas and the US President has already threatened to go off script.

There is a risk that they both dominate the meeting and Xi ends up looking like a host, rather than the architect of a major diplomatic moment.

Of course, Xi may be ready for this. It may even play into his hands.

The Chinese leader has been trying to portray himself as a stable global leader - at this summit he will be flanked by two men embroiled in wars they cannot seem to end.

So any unscripted moment could serve to highlight his preferred role as senior statesman.

For all the attention, this meeting of three men with vastly different agendas is unlikely to yield any significant outcomes.

But the power it projects is important for Xi as he heads towards next year's Communist Party Congress, where he is expected to secure a historic fourth term as leader of the party and country.

He may hope to use this as propaganda at home, given the country is grappling with huge domestic challenges.

A country-wide property crisis has dented consumer confidence. Local governments are heavily in debt. Manufacturing has slowed and more of China's workforce has become dependent on flexible jobs with no pension or social security. One in five young people are thought to be struggling to find work. Frustration and anxiety about the future bubble up routinely.

Xi does not have to deal with elections, and the country has not seen major protests in decades. But he will be concerned about his popularity within the party elite as these problems - and the palpable frustrations they produce - grow.

At a time like this, a photo-op with Putin and Trump may offer him proof that his country's "century of humiliation" is over. China is no longer a rising power, he can argue - rather, it is increasingly shaping the rules of a new era.

articles.title: Trump makes third Supreme Court bid to end Venezuelan migrant protections
articles.summary: Emergency appeal follows a California judge’s ruling that ending their temporary protected status was unlawful.
articles.body:
US President Donald Trump’s administration has asked the Supreme Court to issue an emergency order allowing officials to strip legal protections for hundreds of thousands of Venezuelan migrants, marking the third time it has appealed to the nation’s top judicial body over the issue.

The Department of Justice on Wednesday filed an emergency application asking the Supreme Court to put on hold a federal judge’s ruling that officials lacked the authority to end the Temporary Protected Status (TPS) granted to the migrants under former President Joe Biden.

San Francisco-based US District Judge Edward Chen’s ruling is due to take effect on Friday unless a federal appeals court or the Supreme Court moves to suspend it. The Supreme Court previously paused Chen’s ruling in October 2025.

The Trump administration argued that reinstating TPS for Venezuelans would prevent the administration from carrying out up to 332 removal orders and require it to provide them with work authorisation. It also argued that reinstating the protections would cause “severe and immediate harm”.

If the justices do not intervene again before Friday, the administration could be required to release about 1,800 Venezuelans from detention, federal attorneys wrote.

The plaintiffs who challenged the administration’s actions, including TPS holders and an advocacy group, said that since the previous Supreme Court intervention in the case, Venezuelan TPS holders have been detained, separated from children who are US citizens, deported to Venezuela, and even sent to so-called “third countries” where they have no ties.

The Supreme Court in June backed the administration’s separate actions ending TPS for hundreds of thousands of Haitians and Syrians , giving a boost to the Republican president’s hardline approach towards immigration.

TPS is a designation that lets migrants from countries stricken by war, natural disaster or other catastrophes live and work in the US while it is unsafe for them to return to their home countries.

A person granted TPS cannot be deported, can obtain an employment authorisation document, and may be given travel authorisation. A TPS holder cannot be detained by the US over their immigration status.

The Trump administration has terminated TPS for more than 1 million people from 13 countries, including Venezuela, Haiti, Honduras, Nicaragua, Afghanistan and Syria. But in a change in practice, the administration kept protections in place for nearly 200,000 Salvadorans whose TPS was set to expire by September 9, and for more than 100,000 people from Ukraine and Sudan in October.

Millions of people have fled Venezuela in recent years due to political repression and a crippling economic crisis spurred in part by US sanctions against the government of President Nicolas Maduro .

Before leaving office, the Biden administration had extended TPS for about 600,000 Venezuelans through October 2026.

The State Department currently warns people to reconsider travel to Venezuela due to the risk of crime, kidnapping and poor health infrastructure, among other issues.

articles.title: ICJ to rule on Rohingya genocide case against Myanmar: What’s at stake?
articles.summary: World court to issue key verdict in its first genocide ruling in more than a decade.
articles.body:
The top court of the United Nations is scheduled to rule on whether Myanmar committed genocide against its Rohingya Muslim minority in a case brought by the West African nation of The Gambia.

The International Court of Justice (ICJ) in The Hague is to deliver its verdict on Thursday in what will be its first judgement on the merits of a genocide case in more than a decade.

Legal experts said the ruling could bear on South Africa’s ongoing case accusing Israel of genocide in Gaza, which Israel is contesting.

The Gambia accuses Myanmar of seeking to destroy the Rohingya people during a 2017 military crackdown that forced hundreds of thousands to flee. Myanmar, meanwhile, claims it was responding to attacks by fighters from the Arakan Rohingya Salvation Army (ARSA) on police posts.

What happened to the Rohingya in Myanmar?

Myanmar’s military began what it called clearance operations in Rakhine State in October 2016 and a far larger campaign in August 2017 after attacks on police posts by a Rohingya armed group. About 10,000 Rohingya were killed and 740,000 forced to flee to Bangladesh, the UN estimated.

UN investigators found that soldiers razed hundreds of villages, carried out mass killings and routinely raped and gang-raped Rohingya women, girls and boys. They said the sexual violence indicated genocidal intent.

The military itself has announced convictions in only two cases brought after the violence. However, in one, seven soldiers jailed for killing 10 Rohingya men and boys at Inn Din village were freed after serving less than a year of their 10-year sentences.

In 1982, long before the crackdown, Myanmar excluded the Rohingya from its 135 recognised ethnic groups, calling them immigrant Bengalis despite many families having lived in Myanmar for generations. Nearly all Rohingya have been denied citizenship since then, making them the world’s largest stateless group .

Since fighting with the military resumed in 2023, the Arakan Army, an ethnic Rakhine armed group, has taken most of the state. The Office of the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights said in August that both forces have committed widespread and systematic abuses against the Rohingya, accusing the Arakan Army of torture, sexual violence and forced recruitment.

The UN said those abuses have driven more than 155,000 Rohingya into Bangladesh since early 2024, taking the refugee population there up to about 1.2 million.

Nearly all the refugees live in crowded camps in the Cox’s Bazar District, where they are dependent on international aid that has fallen sharply in recent years, particularly since United States President Donald Trump’s administration slashed foreign aid in 2025. Most refugees now receive smaller food rations, and many camp schools have closed. The Office of the UN High Commissioner for Refugees warned that recent arrivals often lack sufficient food, clean water and healthcare.

Why did The Gambia take Myanmar to the ICJ?

The Gambia said it brought the case after decades of persecution of the Rohingya that culminated in the 2017 operation, which it argued breached the 1948 Genocide Convention.

The Muslim-majority nation of 2.5 million people filed the case in November 2019 on behalf of the 57-member Organisation of Islamic Cooperation (OIC). The case was led by Abubacarr Tambadou, then The Gambia’s attorney general and justice minister.

In January 2020, the court ordered Myanmar to take emergency measures to prevent genocidal acts.

Myanmar initially argued that The Gambia, which was not directly involved in the conflict, could not bring the case. But in 2022, judges ruled that it could because both countries are parties to the convention, under which all signatories are obligated to prevent and punish genocide.

Hearings on the merits of the case followed in January this year with seven states – including Canada, France and the United Kingdom – backing The Gambia.

What exactly is the ICJ being asked to decide?

The judges must decide whether Myanmar, as a state, committed genocide against the Rohingya, thereby breaching the 1948 Convention on the Prevention and Punishment of the Crime of Genocide.

The ICJ passes judgements on state actions. It does not rule on the criminal guilt of individual soldiers or commanders.

Under the convention, “genocide” refers to acts such as killing and causing serious harm committed with intent to destroy, wholly or partly, a national, ethnic, racial or religious group.

Evidence that a state has committed atrocities is not enough. The court must also find they were carried out with specific intent to destroy a group. Such intent can be shown through direct statements or orders or inferred from a pattern of conduct.

The Gambia argued that genocidal intent is the only reasonable inference from Myanmar’s conduct.

Myanmar, meanwhile, said it was conducting a legitimate counterterrorism operation against Rohingya fighters, not targeting Rohingya people as a whole.

What would a genocide finding mean for the Rohingya?

A genocide finding would formally recognise the harm the Rohingya have suffered but may do little in the short term for the more than one million victims of violence and displacement, said Michael Becker, an international law professor at Trinity College Dublin and a former ICJ legal officer.

The Gambia wants the court to order Myanmar to ensure displaced Rohingya can return safely to their land, compensate them, and replace or rebuild destroyed homes and property.

Becker told Al Jazeera the court may impose those demands only partly or in general terms, leaving Myanmar to decide how to comply with them.

Such an outcome would “surely be disappointing” to those who are sceptical that the government would fulfil those demands in good faith, he said.

“Even if the ICJ were to order far-reaching forms of relief, the political conditions on the ground in Myanmar are not amenable to realising that relief anytime soon,” Becker said.

He said a finding would instead have to be used to pressure Myanmar diplomatically.

William Schabas, an international law professor at Middlesex University in the UK, said the measures that The Gambia was seeking on behalf of the Rohingya were “robust” even though they fell short of demanding citizenship, which would end their statelessness.

“Assuming Myanmar implements the conclusions, this will indeed have significant positive effects on the security, dignity and livelihoods of the Rohingya in Myanmar,” Schabas told Al Jazeera.

What could the ruling mean for future genocide cases?

The Myanmar ruling will be the first final judgement out of five genocide cases pending before the ICJ.

Becker said the outcome could clarify the court’s longstanding “only reasonable inference” test. Under it, judges infer genocidal intent from a pattern of conduct only if no other reasonable explanation fits.

He said the court’s two rulings on the Balkan wars left it unclear whether genocide could be deemed to occur alongside armed conflict, which he said was “an unduly restrictive standard”.

Thursday’s judgement could instead treat armed conflict as an alternative explanation for a party’s conduct, rather than an automatic bar to establishing genocidal intent, he said.

According to Schabas, the ruling will “have very dramatic effects” on the outcome of the other pending cases, particularly the case against Israel.

“In my opinion, the South African case against Israel is much stronger than the case of Gambia against Myanmar. If Gambia wins against Myanmar, we can be confident that South Africa will prevail over Israel,” he said.
