articles.title: A woman bought a £4,550 Cartier bracelet from Harrods but returned it because it was too small; the luxury retailer refused a refund, claiming she had scratched it, but a court ordered it to pay her £5,131
articles.summary: A woman who spent £4,550 on a Cartier bracelet as a birthday treat has won a court battle against luxury department store Harrods after it refused to
articles.body: A woman who spent £4,550 on a Cartier bracelet as a birthday treat has won a court battle against luxury department store Harrods after it refused to refund her money over allegations of damage. Georgia Romain, a hypnotherapist from Kingston upon Thames, London, had ordered the 18-carat gold bracelet online but decided to return it in July 2025 after finding that it was too small for her wrist. However, Harrods rejected the return, claiming that the jewellery had scratches and could no longer be resold. Romain challenged the retailer's evidence and eventually took the dispute to court without legal representation. The judge ruled in her favour, ordering Harrods to pay £5,131, including the original purchase price, interest and court fees.Woman returns Cartier bracelet after finding it too smallRomain had reportedly saved for years to purchase the Cartier Love bracelet, which she had planned as a birthday treat for herself. However, after receiving the 18-carat gold piece, she found that it was too small and did not fit her wrist properly.Having purchased it through Harrods' online store, she arranged to return the bracelet in its original box in July 2025, expecting a refund.The retailer subsequently informed her that the return had been rejected because the bracelet allegedly contained scratches and defects. Harrods also warned that the jewellery would be transferred to its lost property department unless she reclaimed it within 30 days.The decision left Romain without the bracelet or the money she had paid for it, prompting her to challenge the retailer's assessment of the returned item.Harrods claims bracelet had scratches and could not be resoldThe dispute centred on a pre-inspection video recorded by Harrods after receiving the returned bracelet. The retailer's customer service team used the footage to identify what it described as scratches and defects on the jewellery's soft gold surface.Harrods maintained that the bracelet had been damaged and argued that it could no longer be resold in that condition.However, Romain questioned whether the bracelet shown in the inspection footage was actually the one she had purchased. She pointed out that the video did not display the item's unique serial number and also suggested that the bracelet being examined appeared thicker than the one she had ordered.In an email to the retailer, she asked how she could be certain that the footage showed her bracelet without seeing its serial number. She requested evidence linking the alleged scratches to the specific item she had returned.According to the court proceedings, Harrods' subsequent response did not address her concerns about the missing serial number. Instead, the retailer formally rejected the return and informed her that the bracelet was legally her property.Judge questions Harrods' evidence over alleged scratchesAfter failing to resolve the dispute with the retailer, Romain brought a claim against Harrods at London's Mayors and City County Court, representing herself without legal assistance.Deputy District Judge Elaine Vignoli ruled in her favour, finding that Harrods had failed to establish, on the balance of probabilities, that the bracelet was returned with the alleged scratches.The judge questioned why the retailer had not provided the evidence Romain had reasonably requested, particularly footage showing the bracelet's unique serial number alongside the alleged damage.She described Harrods' position in its email correspondence as "frankly staggering", noting that Romain had made a reasonable request concerning an item of considerable value.Harrods' lawyers argued that the bracelet would have been secured safely and handled carefully throughout the return process. However, the judge said there was no evidence before the court to substantiate that assurance.She concluded that the retailer had not proved that the scratches were present when it received the bracelet from Romain.Judge says she would happily take home supposedly worthless braceletThe court also examined Harrods' argument that the alleged scratches had made the 18-carat gold bracelet worthless because it could no longer be resold.Judge Vignoli questioned this position, particularly because the retailer had not provided convincing evidence demonstrating how the alleged damage had affected the jewellery's value.In a pointed observation during the proceedings, she said: "If it is genuinely worthless I would happily take it home with me."The judge also described the bracelet as a "rather pretty, luxurious item" while discussing the retailer's claim that it had become worthless because of minor scuffs and scratches.She ultimately concluded that Harrods had failed to provide sufficient evidence to support its defence and ruled in favour of the customer.Harrods ordered to pay £5,131 to customerFollowing the ruling, Harrods was ordered to pay Romain £4,550, representing the original cost of the bracelet. With accumulated interest and court fees, the total amount payable came to £5,131.Romain described herself as "very relieved" after the outcome and said she would not shop at the luxury retailer again."I'm never buying from Harrods again," she said after the hearing.She also explained that she had spent years saving for the bracelet and had wanted to buy it as a special birthday present for herself."I was saving for years, I wanted to treat myself," she said, adding that she would return to saving money rather than making another expensive purchase.You use AI every day. articles.title: Reagan’s peace through strength won the Cold War. Can America do it again?
articles.summary: Can the United States rebuild its arsenal again? Roger Zakheim's new book recalls how Ronald Reagan's defense buildup won the Cold War against Russia.
articles.body: From the Cuban Missile Crisis forward, the United States faced a drive by the Soviet Union to achieve nuclear superiority over America and its allies. The Soviet buildup began as the U.S. entered the quagmire of the Vietnam War. The Russians had reached the cusp of actual superiority in nuclear arsenals when Ronald Reagan beat then-President Jimmy Carter and launched a defense buildup unmatched in the peacetime history of America. The story of that buildup, and of how Reagan and his team of defense and national security advisers designed the policy and sold it to the public and then Congress, is told in a riveting new book by Roger Zakheim, "Peace Through Strength: How Reagan’s Military Buildup Won the Cold War." TRUMP HOLDS THE NUCLEAR CARDS TO PLAY AGAINST CHINA AND RUSSIA ON ARMS CONTROL Zakheim is the director of the Ronald Reagan Institute, a position he took after careers at the D.C. law firm Covington & Burling LLP and as general counsel and deputy staff director of the House Armed Services Committee. Zakheim brings actual Hill experience and a lawyer’s eye to the details of the more-than-a-decade-long crusade by Reagan to recover America’s military strength. That effort began almost immediately after President Gerald Ford’s defeat by Carter in 1976 and is intertwined with Reagan’s long march to the 1980 Republican Party nomination and subsequent election and eight years in office. Those who did not live through those years will be surprised by the breadth and depth of Reagan’s commitment to rebuilding the American arsenal during his long climb to the presidency. The entire intellectual architecture of the "peace through strength" network is reviewed by Zakheim. Names that were familiar to most of the Beltway and its ecosystem four decades ago — from Richard Allen to William Van Cleave, from now-obscure figures like Fred Iklé to the still (and justifiably) famous like John Lehman — appear and play their parts. Zakheim has carefully reconstructed the drama, and all of its players are on stage for long or short periods. All to the end that President Reagan envisioned: winning the Cold War and preserving the peace between superpowers by paying for an arsenal so complete that no hostile power dared to challenge America at home or around the world where its vital interests were involved. REPUBLICANS NEED A REAGAN-STYLE VISION TO WIN THE BATTLE OVER AMERICA'S FUTURE The defense buildup Reagan launched and oversaw was a complex and expensive undertaking. It succeeded only with the assistance of such stalwarts in his administration as Secretary of Defense Caspar "Cap" Weinberger and his deputy, Frank Carlucci, and on the Hill, such as Sens. John Tower, R-Texas, and Sam Nunn, D-Ga. There were defeats along the way, such as the battle over the MX missile, and incredible triumphs, such as the deployment of Pershing II missiles in Europe and the original commitment to the Strategic Defense Initiative. But both Reagan and then-President George H.W. Bush persevered, and the incredible strength and productivity of free markets and free minds triumphed. The arsenal Reagan and Bush built, however, has a shelf life. While Congress can and has mandated, for example, that the Navy build and maintain 11 nuclear-powered aircraft carriers, it cannot simply decree that those carriers afloat continue in service beyond the years their nuclear cores are designed for, nor can Congress expedite their replacement. No part of the American arsenal is immune to the ravages of Father Time. A near-continuous refurbishing and resupply of America’s defenses is required. The entire national debt in 1981 was less than $1 trillion. Today it is more than $40 trillion. IS THE US ALREADY LOSING TO CHINA ON INNOVATION, LOGISTICS AND RAPID RESUPPLY? President Trump has secured the funding for the beginning of the refurbishment and renewal of the national security infrastructure, but the continuation of the rebuild is very much in doubt as the new Democratic majorities arrive in January. There is no Sam Nunn across the aisle from such Republican stalwarts of defense as Mississippi’s Sen. Roger Wicker and Arkansas' Sen. Tom Cotton. Most of the new arrivals on Team Blue want to spend much more on social programs and much less on defense, even though Russia’s enduring enmity toward the U.S. has been matched and exceeded by that of the People’s Republic of China. As the Republican Congress enters its final 50 days, by far its most important task is to preserve the start of the rearmament of America. Zakheim’s book has arrived just as an intense debate over a supplemental appropriation to the Pentagon is underway on the Hill. US RAMPS NUCLEAR WEAPONS PRODUCTION TO COLD WAR LEVELS AS CHINA PURSUES ‘UNPRECEDENTED’ BUILDUP "Peace Through Strength" is a prod to the Republicans, and especially those wrapping up long and distinguished careers, to end this Congress on a high note, recalling 1981, when President Reagan sought and received a supplemental spending bill to begin his rebuild that would go on to accomplish such great things and preserve the peace. The book should also inform every would-be president from both parties. The 1980 campaign (which began almost immediately after the 1978 midterms) was very much focused on America’s defenses, from its hardware on hand to the then-dire state of the all-volunteer force. HEGSETH UNLEASHES TRUMP'S 'ARSENAL OF FREEDOM' WITH WARNING TO DEFENSE GIANTS The country needs another such presidential campaign as the complexity of the threats facing the country has grown ever more menacing over the past two decades. America summoned the will to preserve the peace in the 1980s because of leadership that began with an out-of-office governor contemplating an unlikely second try for the White House and his team of advisers who helped craft his message and campaign. Hewitt launched his eponymous radio show from Los Angeles in 1990. articles.title: ‘Displacement by design’: Trump’s Gaza peace plan a failure, aid groups say
articles.summary: With two million Palestinians confined to an area of less than 130sq km, UN-backed Gaza peace plan has collapsed.
articles.body:
One year after the United Nations Security Council endorsed the Trump administration’s 20-point Comprehensive Plan to end the Gaza Conflict, a coalition of five prominent international aid organisations has issued a damning assessment.

As Israeli forces launched a new ground offensive in central Gaza this week, advancing with tanks west of its “Yellow Line”, and issued new forced evacuation orders, in violation of the peace plan, the Danish Refugee Council, Norwegian Refugee Council, Oxfam, Refugees International and Save the Children, released a humanitarian scorecard which grades the plan at just four out of 26 possible points. The plan scored a zero on humanitarian access and earned just one point for civilian protection.

Despite the Gaza Peace Plan’s explicit prohibition against territorial occupation in Gaza – and its requirement that Israeli forces withdraw – the Israeli military “Yellow Line” has moved further west, expanding control of Gaza territory from 58 percent at the start of the ceasefire 13 months ago, to 65 percent today, according to OCHA. Israel itself has said it controls 70 percent of the territory, a UN official told the UN Security Council in June this year.

Palestinians are not allowed to cross the line, so this expansion has confined roughly 2.1 million Palestinians to just 128sq km (49 sq miles), according to OCHA last month, squeezing 16,000 people into each square km. More recent analysis suggests it may be even smaller. Recent map analysis by US news group NPR found the confinement area is now just 109sq km (42 sq miles), creating a population density of nearly 19,300 people per sq km.

Ramy Abdu, founder and chairman of the Euro-Mediterranean Human Rights Monitor, warned that Israel is carrying out unlawful acquisition of territory by force.

The human cost has been devastating, agencies say, with at least 1,650 Palestinians killed and 5,975 wounded since the “ceasefire” was declared in October last year.

Earlier this week, Shaun Hughes, World Food Programme ( WFP ) country director for Palestine, told journalists: “When you’re in Gaza, it does not feel like a ceasefire. Israeli military control across nearly 70 per cent of Gaza means that people have almost no space to grow their own food. Fishing in the sea is prohibited and also life-threatening. Unemployment is over 80 per cent, so without humanitarian assistance, people have little or no alternate means of survival.”

Lilu Thapa, executive director for the Middle East, Asia and Europe at the Danish Refugee Council, said: “Palestinians in Gaza are being confined as the “Yellow Line” expands. This is displacement by design, and a ceasefire that allows it is a ceasefire in name only.”

The diplomatic framework overseeing this crisis, specifically the Board of Peace and International Stabilization Force (ISF) established by United States President Donald Trump, has drawn intense scrutiny from human rights experts who accuse the body of abandoning its mandate.

“Euro-Med Human Rights Monitor believes that, from the moment of its establishment, the Board of Peace represented a serious infringement on the Palestinian people’s right to self-determination, both in its composition and in the powers entrusted to it,” Abdu told Al Jazeera.

The Board, chaired by the US, operates without any meaningful Palestinian representation, Abdu said.

“Instead, it has effectively become a political shield for Israel’s occupation and its crimes, contributing to the perpetuation of genocidal conditions while providing political cover for grave violations of international law,” Abdu told Al Jazeera. “The available evidence supports describing the Board’s role as a form of functional normalisation of genocide and starvation.”

Mohsen Abu Ramadan, a board member of the Palestinian NGOs Network, said: “Regretfully, the Board of Peace failed the international community and continues to ‎‎provide political cover for ongoing genocide and atrocities.”

The peace plan announced last year stipulated that a minimum of 600 UN-coordinated humanitarian aid trucks would be allowed to enter Gaza daily. In reality, an average of just 49 UN-coordinated trucks entered the Strip each day in September.

Only two percent of these limited convoys carried medical supplies, leading to critical shortages and deaths from treatable illnesses.

Instead, Israeli authorities have increasingly prioritised the entry of commercial trucks carrying expensive goods that the impoverished population cannot afford to buy.

During the week of October 12, of 315 commercial trucks which entered Gaza, 223 carried food and 51 carried non-essential items. Only 12 carried hygiene and shelter materials and just a single truck carried medical supplies.

Israel has cited “dual use” restrictions, which restrict the entry of products and goods which have a military as well as a civilian purpose.

Jan Egeland, CEO of the Norwegian Refugee Council, said that the crisis stems from political decisions. “The suffering of Gaza’s 2.1 million people is not inevitable. The world must stop accepting it,” Egeland said. Oxfam America President Abby Maxman noted that the reality on the ground is a “direct result of policy choices made in Israel, the US and at the UN.”

As Gaza enters its fourth winter of displacement, the shelter crisis has reached breaking point.

While donors have pledged about $18bn for Gaza via the Board of Peace, more than a year after the ceasefire was declared, reconstruction has yet to begin and nearly 1.4m Palestinians are living in makeshift shelters.

A recent winter storm flooded more than 70,000 tents in a single day, resulting in the drowning of an infant and the deaths of five displaced people. While stocks of tents and blankets inside Gaza are virtually exhausted, more than 150,000 tents and 500,000 blankets are locked outside the territory’s borders, waiting for permission to enter.

“What greater moral and legal outrage could there be than invoking so-called dual-use restrictions to prevent the entry of tents and basic hygiene supplies as winter approaches?” Abdu told Al Jazeera.

Save the Children International CEO Inger Ashing said: “One year ago, the world was promised that Gaza’s children would finally see safety, relief and a chance to rebuild their lives. Instead, they are colder, hungrier, more traumatised and more at risk than they were before.”

Jeremy Konyndyk, president of Refugees International, called on international backers to act. “The United States and other UN Security Council members must use their leverage to ensure those obligations are met,” he said.

With the medical evacuation system collapsing, Gaza’s health ministry has reported that 2,027 patients have died while awaiting transfer and 21,000 remain on waiting lists.

Abdu outlined five complementary paths towards accountability, including the enforcement of International Criminal Court (ICC) arrest warrants for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and other officials, the continuation of International Court of Justice (ICJ) genocide proceedings against Israel and the pursuit of universal jurisdiction in national courts. He also called for regional arms embargoes on Israel and pressed the UN Security Council to hold a public briefing to examine the Board of Peace’s failures.

“No institution, regardless of its name, mandate or political sponsorship, can legitimately claim to be advancing peace while allowing the killing of civilians, the destruction of the conditions necessary for human survival and the expansion of an unlawful occupation to continue unchecked,” Abdu told Al Jazeera.

Board blames Israeli ‘political indecision’

Al Jazeera contacted the Board of Peace for a response to these claims. In response, head of communications Brad Klapper sent us the Board’s latest official report via WhatsApp. He did not address the specific allegations about encroachment on territory or refusal of permission for aid trucks to enter the enclave.

When pressed by Al Jazeera for direct answers to these inquiries, Klapper stated: “This is your reply. You have our assessment of where things stand.”

The report provided by Klapper included an acknowledgement of the failures to implement the peace plan in Gaza but appeared to place the blame on Israeli political indecision in several areas.

“…Implementation on the ground, however, has been limited, pending decisions that need to be taken by the parties… as soon as the necessary decisions are adopted by the Government of Israel,” the report states in one part.

Later, it also states: “The absence of decisions by the Government of Israel on the necessary conditions and arrangements for the training, deployment and return of civilian police to Gaza continues to impede full implementation of the Comprehensive Plan.”

Paragraph 49 of the report states: “That process, which relies not on trust but on verified results, cannot begin while the requisite decisions remain pending. The Board of Peace therefore urges Israel… to take without delay the decisions required for the training, deployment and return of the civilian police and for the entry of the NCAG and the ISF”, referring to National Committee for the Administration of Gaza (NCAG) and the International Stabilization Force (ISF) which are provided for under the peace plan, but which have yet to be allowed to enter Gaza.

The report also highlights that Hamas and Palestinian factions accepted a 15-point roadmap on July 30 to relinquish their weapons and transfer full authority to a transitional administration.

However, it notes that execution mechanisms for this remain paralysed and states that the absence of decisions by the Israeli government continues to impede the plan.

Concluding its report, the Board states in the report: “A ceasefire that delivers nothing visible cannot be sustained indefinitely. The people of Gaza have paid the highest price for this war and should not be asked to pay again for delay.”
